title: Audi explains the $300,000 premium for its Nuvolari supercar over the Lamborghini Temerario
extract: Audi says the Nuvolari earns its roughly $700,000 price through a carbon-fibre body, active Formula 1-inspired aerodynamics producing more than 400kg of downforce, larger brakes and a more sophisticated predictive quattro system. Its 987hp hybrid V8 makes it more powerful than the Temerario on which it is based, while production is limited to 499 cars.

title: Toyota's tiny rear-wheel-drive S-FR sports car could be revived as a kei coupe
extract: A Japanese report suggests Toyota may revive the S-FR name as a compact rear-wheel-drive sports car built to kei-car dimensions, potentially using a turbocharged 660cc engine and manual gearbox. The idea draws on Daihatsu's running K-Open development prototypes, although neither company has confirmed a production model.

title: Wine 11.22 adds x86 AVX emulation for Windows software on ARM64
extract: Wine 11.22 adds Advanced Vector Extensions support to its x86 emulation path on ARM64, helping Windows applications that assume AVX is available run through ARM64EC builds. The release also updates Unicode locale data, improves address-space randomisation and includes 34 bug fixes.

title: Cloudflare open-sources Kitesurf, its lightweight browser built for AI agents
extract: Cloudflare has released Kitesurf under the Apache 2.0 licence. Built on Cloudflare Workers, the stateless browser can parse HTML, handle CSS and execute JavaScript without a full browser container, aiming to give agents a lighter and more scalable way to interact with websites.

title: AMD's openSIL reaches production on sixth-generation EPYC Venice processors
extract: AMD has confirmed that openSIL, its open-source alternative to proprietary AGESA silicon initialisation, has met its production goal with sixth-generation EPYC Venice. AMD says no Venice platform has booted without openSIL and expects to publish the Venice code within a quarter of launch, opening further possibilities for Coreboot-based systems.

title: KDE Frameworks 6.32 fixes a 15-year-old bug in USB file-copy notifications
extract: KDE Frameworks 6.32 corrects a long-standing issue where the completion notification for copying files to removable USB storage appeared when data had reached the local cache, rather than when it had actually been written to the device. The fix uses sync_file_range, alongside broader Baloo, KArchive and Kirigami improvements.

title: AMD uses AI agents and HRX Loom to port 50 language models to client GPUs in days
extract: An AMD engineering experiment brought 50 Hugging Face models spanning 18 architectures to AMD client GPUs in roughly three to four days using HRX Loom and an AI-agent workflow. The team reported 1.5–2.1x faster 32K-token prompt processing than llama.cpp's ROCm backend and 1.9x over its Vulkan backend, although Loom remains experimental.

title: XRAID is released as a new parity RAID implementation for the XFS filesystem
extract: Linux developer Christoph Hellwig has publicly released XRAID, a declustered-parity RAID implementation integrated with XFS and aimed particularly at zoned storage such as shingled magnetic-recording drives. Its design also works with conventional disks and SSDs, with the developer reporting write speeds up to 20 times faster than mdraid in some cases.

title: One for Sorrow by Favel Parrett review: a finely crafted novel of wartime betrayal and desire
extract: Favel Parrett's novel is set in Nazi-occupied Trondheim and follows a lonely boy who finds a surrogate father in his new teacher, while the teacher begins an affair with the boy's mother. The Guardian praises the book's spare prose and subtle portrayal of grief, family silence and the emotional consequences of wartime intimacy.

title: The best books to read in November and December: new paperbacks from Benjamin Myers, Jeanette Winterson and John Updike
extract: The Guardian's new paperback roundup ranges from Benjamin Myers's imaginative novel about actor Klaus Kinski to Rabih Alameddine's buoyant family story, Glasgow-set crime fiction by Frances Crawford, a newly translated Henning Mankell novel and Ian Buruma's history of wartime Berlin. It offers a varied set of fiction, crime, history and memoir recommendations.

title: This Cursed Beautiful Land by Evan Gershkovich review: a reporter's account of imprisonment in Russia
extract: Evan Gershkovich recounts his arrest on fabricated espionage charges while reporting in Russia, 18 months in prison and eventual release in a 2024 prisoner exchange. The review finds his account of prison life compelling and illuminating, while noting the limits of analysing a country from behind bars.

title: Inside the 42-year journey to bring William Gibson's Neuromancer to the screen
extract: WIRED speaks with the creators and cast of Apple's long-awaited Neuromancer adaptation about the decades of failed attempts to film William Gibson's 1984 novel. The team discusses Gibson's involvement, the expanded Tessier-Ashpool storyline, practical retro-futurist sets built partly in Japan and the challenge of creating a world that feels distinct from the many works the book inspired.

title: Cunk on Cinema review: Diane Morgan's mockumentary is a gloriously stupid guide to film history
extract: Diane Morgan returns as Philomena Cunk for a three-part comic history of cinema, baffling experts and filmmakers including Benedict Cumberbatch, Mark Kermode and Michael Bay with surreal questions and mangled film references. The Guardian praises its relentless gag rate and deadpan absurdity, with Charlie Brooker and his long-time collaborators continuing to write the series.

title: Gentle Monster to Conclave: seven films worth watching on television this week
extract: The Guardian's weekly film guide highlights a mix of recent drama, mystery and historical storytelling, led by Marie Kreutzer's Gentle Monster with Léa Seydoux and Edward Berger's twisty papal thriller Conclave starring Ralph Fiennes. The selection also includes Kurosawa's epic Ran and films ranging from Eileen to The Dead Don't Hurt.

title: Darth Vader's original lightsaber sells for a record $4.875 million
extract: The lightsaber used by Darth Vader in The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi, including the iconic 'I am your father' sequence, sold for $4.875 million at Heritage Auctions. The sale set a record for an on-screen Star Wars prop, surpassing the previous record for Luke Skywalker's lightsaber and severed hand.
